h1: Keg couplers and fittings explained for bar teams
title: Keg Couplers and Fittings Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: Keg coupler types, the parts inside a coupler and the fittings between keg and tap, explained for bar teams, with the checks that stop leaks.
teaser: A keg coupler has two seals, two valves and a safety valve. Most leaks at a bar come from one of them.
standfirst: The coupler is the fitting that connects a keg to the gas and the beer line. Bar staff handle it every day and rarely look inside it. Knowing the types, the parts and the fittings around it prevents most leaks, foamy pours and damaged kegs. Here is what a bar team needs to know.
sections: The coupler does two jobs at once

A keg has a single valve on top, called the spear or extractor. The coupler locks onto it and opens two paths. Gas flows in through one side, pressing on the beer. Beer flows out through the other, up a tube that reaches the bottom of the keg.

When you press the coupler handle down, a probe pushes open the keg valve and both paths connect. Lift the handle and both close. That is why you should always lift the handle to off before twisting the coupler away.

Kegs use different valve designs, so couplers come in several types. The ones bar teams meet most often are:

  • S type: the European Sankey, widely used by European breweries.
  • D type: the American Sankey, used on most US kegs.
  • A type: a slider style used on some German kegs.
  • U type: used on some Irish stout kegs.

Other types exist for particular breweries and countries. Kegs reach Indian bars from many suppliers, so check the coupler type with each brewery before the first delivery. A wrong coupler will not seat. Forcing it damages the seals on both parts.

• Probe and bottom seal. The probe opens the keg valve. The seal around it stops beer and gas leaking at the keg. This washer wears out fastest.
  • Gas inlet with a non return valve. Lets gas in and stops beer flowing back into the gas line and regulator if pressure drops.
  • Beer outlet with a check valve. Stops beer in the line draining back into the keg when the coupler is removed.
  • Pressure relief valve. A small ring or knob that vents gas if pressure inside the coupler gets too high. Pull it to release pressure safely before servicing.

Beer backing up into a regulator is a costly repair. A working non return valve is cheap insurance.

Seals are made of rubber compounds that harden with age, heat and cleaning chemicals. A seal that looks fine can still have lost its spring. Press it with a fingernail: a good seal gives and recovers, a tired one stays dented.
The fittings between keg and tap

From the coupler, the beer line runs to the tap through a short chain of fittings: a tail piece pushed into the tubing, a hex nut with a washer connecting it to the coupler or shank, sometimes a foam on beer detector and finally the shank and faucet. Every joint has a washer or an O ring. Every washer is a possible leak.

Hose clamps matter too. Stepless ear clamps grip evenly and do not loosen with temperature changes. Screw type clips can cut into soft tubing if over tightened. Whatever the bar uses, check them during each line clean. Our guide to draught line cleaning lists what to inspect.

1. Look at every coupler bottom seal. Replace any that is flattened, cracked or hard.
  2. Spray each gas joint and coupler with soapy water. Bubbles mean a gas leak.
  3. Check for beer weeping at hex nuts and tail pieces. A sticky ring around a joint means a washer has failed.
  4. Pull each coupler's relief valve briefly to make sure it moves freely.
  5. Look for beer in the gas lines. If you see any, a non return valve has failed.

Keep a small box of spare coupler seals and hex nut washers behind the bar. They cost little and turn a leak into a two minute fix.

Couplers sit in the beer path, so they need cleaning with the lines. Many systems clean through a cleaning cap or socket that fits the coupler in place of a keg, so solution flows through the coupler as well as the line. If your system cleans from the tap end only, the coupler body and probe can be missed.

Every few months, strip each coupler, soak the parts in line cleaner, rinse and check the valves move freely. Dried beer in a check valve can make it stick open or shut. In hot humid bars this happens sooner than in a cool cellar.

A keg at serving pressure holds a lot of stored energy. Never hit a coupler with a mallet to make it seat. Never try to remove or repair a keg spear. If a coupler will not go on, check the type and look for damage on the keg valve. Send damaged kegs back to the brewery with a note.

Store kegs upright and secure them in the cold room so they cannot fall. A 50 litre steel keg weighs over 60 kg when full.

Your first step: this week, take every coupler behind your bar, check its type against the kegs you use and look at its bottom seal. Replace any seal that is not soft and round.
faqs: What is the difference between S and D type couplers?
S type is the European Sankey design and D type the American Sankey. They look similar but are not interchangeable.
Why is my keg coupler leaking?
Usually a worn or missing bottom seal, a coupler not fully engaged or a loose hex nut. Check the seal first.
What does the ring on a keg coupler do?
It is a pressure relief valve. Pulling it vents gas from the coupler safely before servicing.
